title: Chapter 45 — The Interior Designer & Architect
intro: The specifier relationship — how architects and interior designers influence appliance selection and the partnership model.

sections.title: The Specifier's Power
sections.content:
Interior designers and architects do not buy appliances — they specify them. And specification is often the final word. When an architect puts Sub-Zero columns on the drawing, the homeowner rarely overrides that decision.

This makes designers and architects the highest-leverage relationships in your trade channel. One designer specifying your recommended products on 10 kitchens per year is worth more than 100 walk-in ups. The challenge is that they are also the hardest to win — they have established supplier relationships and they guard their client relationships carefully.

sections.title: What They Need From You
sections.content:
Technical accuracy above all. A designer who specifies a panel-ready dishwasher based on your recommendation and then discovers it does not fit the cabinetry will never trust you again. Verify every dimension, every panel spec, every clearance requirement before you hand it over.

They also need responsiveness. Designers work on tight project timelines. When they email asking for the cutout dimensions on a Wolf range at 4 PM, they need the answer that evening — not tomorrow morning. The designer who cannot get specs from you quickly will find someone who can.

Finally, they need you to coordinate with their other trades. The cabinetmaker needs panel specs. The electrician needs circuit requirements. The plumber needs water line locations. You should be the single source of truth for all appliance-related requirements on the project.

sections.title: Building the Relationship
sections.content:
Start by attending NKBA (National Kitchen & Bath Association) chapter meetings. Show up consistently. Offer to present on a product topic — 'What is new in ventilation' or 'Panel-ready integration best practices.' Position yourself as the appliance expert for the design community.

Invite designers to your showroom for private product training sessions. After hours, with food, and focused on the products they specify most often. Let them touch the products, open the doors, feel the hardware. Hands-on experience converts better than any spec sheet.

Create a designer resource package: spec sheets, cutout dimensions, panel requirements, and installation guides organized by brand and category. Make it easy for them to specify your recommended products. The designer who has your spec package on their desk will use it because it saves them time.
